citation: Obuchowski NA, Subhas N, Schoenhagen P. Testing for interchangeability of imaging tests. Acad Radiol 2014;21(11):1483-1489.
problem: How to show that a new imaging test can replace an existing one when no reference standard is available.
method: Interchangeability (individual equivalence): compare the disagreement between new and existing tests with the disagreement of the existing test with itself on repeated occasions or readers; applies to categorical and quantitative results.
data: Two worked examples: semiautomated versus manual CT aortic-annulus sizing for TAVR; MRI versus CT acetabular version.
main_result: Semiautomated sizing agreed with manual in 87.6%, yet interchanging it would add 1.7%-12.2% to the frequency of disagreement; replacing CT by MRI adds 2.0-3.1 degrees beyond CT's own differences; agreement or correlation alone is not sufficient evidence.
relevance: Closest imaging-statistics precedent for kappa: kappa relates between-version disagreement to within-version error, as interchangeability compares new-versus-old with old-versus-old disagreement (its index is the excess, a difference; kappa is a ratio; corrected 13 Oct from the full text). Recommendation (2), between-version limits of agreement set against repeat-scan limits, is an interchangeability test. A QIBA-statistics reviewer would expect it next to the VIM compatibility citation.
not_established: No model updates or longitudinal change; its denominator is replicate (precision) disagreement, whereas kappa uses same-version change error against a reference; full text checked 13 Oct (version of record, saved with institutional access).

citation: Barnhart HX, Kosinski AS, Haber MJ. Assessing individual agreement. J Biopharm Stat 2007;17(4):697-719.
venue_and_status: Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics 17(4):697-719; published (Taylor & Francis)
problem: Whether measurement methods or observers can be used interchangeably at the level of the individual.
method: Individual equivalence criteria adapted from the FDA individual bioequivalence guidance; individual equivalence coefficient (IEC) with and without a reference method; coefficient of individual agreement (CIA); method of moments from ANOVA output; nonparametric and bootstrap inference.
data: Five illustrative examples (not imaging-specific).
main_result: States that interchangeability is established only if individual measurements from different methods are similar to replicated measurements from the same method; proposes the IEC and the CIA.
relevance: Statistical primary source for indices that scale between-method disagreement by within-method disagreement; kappa should be positioned relative to the IEC, CIA and individual bioequivalence, stating what differs (denominator is error of change against a reference).
not_established: Requires replicate measurements per method; not imaging; full text not read.

citation: deSouza NM, van der Lugt A, Deroose CM, Alberich-Bayarri A, Bidaut L, Fournier L, et al.; European Society of Radiology; European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer. Standardised lesion segmentation for imaging biomarker quantitation: a consensus recommendation from ESR and EORTC. Insights Imaging 2022;13(1):159.
venue_and_status: Insights into Imaging 13(1):159; published (Springer, open access)
problem: Criteria for standardised lesion segmentation for quantitative imaging biomarkers were unavailable.
method: Modified Delphi process (four rounds; 58, 50, 39 and 44 respondents) run by the EIBALL subcommittee of the ESR and the EORTC Imaging Group; items with at least 75% agreement became recommendations.
data: Expert survey responses.
main_result: Conclusion and Recommendations list includes: 'Segmentation should always use the same platform (both hardware and software (segmentation method)) for longitudinal measurements.' Also recommends specified reference standards and validation processes for machine- and deep-learning tools.
relevance: European consensus support for the manuscript's currently uncited sentence 'The working rule is to measure every timepoint with the same software.'; complements the QIBA profiles. Co-authored by S. Gatidis (Longitudinal-CT).
not_established: Does not use the word 'version'; the Delphi agreement level for this item was not extracted (Table 2 is an image in the XML); not specific to deep-learning updates.

citation: Isensee F, Jaeger PF, Kohl SAA, Petersen J, Maier-Hein KH. nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation. Nat Methods 2021;18(2):203-211.
problem: Designing a segmentation pipeline for each new dataset is non-trivial and dataset-dependent.
method: Self-configuring U-Net framework: fixed parameters, interdependent rules and empirical decisions set preprocessing, architecture, training and post-processing.
data: 23 public datasets from biomedical segmentation competitions.
main_result: Without manual intervention, nnU-Net surpasses most existing approaches, including specialised ones; released publicly.
relevance: Primary citation of the framework used in the stronger-model replication; the manuscript cites only Isensee 2024 ('nnU-Net revisited', source of ResEnc-M). Reviewers routinely ask for the original.
not_established: Not about updates or longitudinal measurement.

citation: Owen AB. The pigeonhole bootstrap. Ann Appl Stat 2007;1(2):386-411.
venue_and_status: Annals of Applied Statistics 1(2):386-411; published (IMS); accepted version arXiv:0712.1111
problem: Bootstrap inference for data with a crossed (two-way) random-effects structure, where McCullagh (2000) showed no bootstrap is exact.
method: Resample rows and columns of the data matrix independently ('pigeonhole' bootstrap) and study its variance estimate.
data: Theory; recommender-system and information-retrieval examples.
main_result: Mean-consistent variance estimate even in heteroscedastic, unbalanced crossed random-effects models; 'mildly conservative, but not unduly so' (the error-variance contribution is overestimated).
relevance: The replication's two-way bootstrap resamples runs and patients independently, which is this pigeonhole bootstrap for a crossed run-by-patient design; citing it justifies the interval method and implies the two-way intervals are, if anything, mildly conservative.
not_established: Theory for means/linear statistics; percentile intervals for differences of patient-balanced MAEs not specifically studied.

citation: Bertels J, Robben D, Vandermeulen D, Suetens P. Theoretical analysis and experimental validation of volume bias of soft Dice optimized segmentation maps in the context of inherent uncertainty. Med Image Anal 2021;67:101833.
venue_and_status: Medical Image Analysis 67:101833; published; accepted version arXiv:2211.04161
problem: Whether common training losses bias the volumes derived from CNN segmentations.
method: Theoretical analysis linking inherent uncertainty to the optima of cross-entropy and soft Dice; experiments with two U-Net sizes on four medical segmentation tasks; volume-specific analysis and a training-set re-calibration.
data: Four public medical segmentation tasks (including BraTS 2018 and ISLES 2017).
main_result: Soft Dice improves Dice but may introduce a volume bias for tasks with high inherent uncertainty; both losses showed a volume-specific bias that over-estimates small and under-estimates large volumes, smaller when discrimination is better; a simple training-set re-calibration reduced bias and volume-specific errors.
relevance: Mechanism for systematic, size-dependent between-version volume shifts that coexist with Dice gains (both segmenters train on Dice plus cross-entropy); supports the under-segmentation explanation and frames the scalar recalibration maps.
not_established: Single models; no updates, longitudinal change or tumour CT.

citation: Hering A, Westphal M, Gerken A, Almansour H, Maurer M, Geisler B, et al. Improving assessment of lesions in longitudinal CT scans: a bi-institutional reader study on an AI-assisted registration and volumetric segmentation workflow. Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg 2024;19(9):1689-1697.
venue_and_status: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery 19(9):1689-1697; published (Springer, open access)
problem: Efficiency, quality and inter-reader variability of AI-assisted volumetric segmentation of metastases in follow-up CT.
method: Three radiologists from two institutions segmented follow-up lesions manually and with AI-proposed registration and segmentation; Dice against a manual reference; inter-reader ICC (two-way random, absolute agreement), by lesion size.
data: 55 patients with stage IV melanoma (Tuebingen); 126 lymph nodes and 135 soft-tissue metastases.
main_result: Manual inter-reader median Dice 0.80-0.82; inter-reader ICC 0.80 overall but 0.31 for lesions below 10 mm; AI assistance raised ICC to 0.84 (0.77 below 10 mm) and cut interaction time by 33%.
relevance: Melanoma, follow-up-CT reader-variability benchmark from the Longitudinal-CT source group (authors include Gatidis, Peisen, Moltz, Kohlbrandt, Othman). Qualifies the lung-only benchmark limitation and the reference-noise limitation; human Dice near 0.8 frames the U-Net (0.54-0.61) and nnU-Net (0.64-0.76) values.
not_established: Inter-reader on the same scans, not scan-rescan; volume agreement given as ICC, not limits of agreement; patients may overlap with Longitudinal-CT.

citation: Li Q, Liang Y, Huang Q, Zong M, Berman B, Gavrielides MA, Schwartz LH, Zhao B, Petrick N. Volumetry of low-contrast liver lesions with CT: investigation of estimation uncertainties in a phantom study. Med Phys 2016;43(12):6608-6620.
problem: Accuracy and precision of liver-lesion CT volumetry across acquisition conditions.
method: Anthropomorphic abdominal phantom with two liver inserts of 19 synthetic lesions each (6-40 mm, 10-65 HU); two scanners; slice thickness, dose, kernel and pitch varied; two repeated scans per protocol; matched-filter estimator and semi-automatic segmentation; bias, linearity and repeatability coefficients.
data: 6080 matched-filter and about 900 segmentation volume measurements.
main_result: Lesions of 10 mm or less with low contrast had high error and were excluded; repeatability coefficients ranged from about 8% to 75%; grouped bias -3% to 3% in most repeatable conditions; volumetry depended on lesion size, contrast, dose and scanner.
relevance: Repeat-scan volumetry of liver lesions exists, though in a phantom: qualifies 'we found no scan--rescan volumetry for liver, pancreatic or melanoma lesions' and gives a non-lung repeatability scale. FDA/QIBA authors, Medical Physics; a PMB reviewer may know it.
not_established: Phantom with synthetic lesions; no patients, pancreatic or melanoma lesions; full text not retrieved (PMC returned abstract only).

citation: Zhao B, Lee SM, Lee HJ, Tan Y, Qi J, Persigehl T, Mozley DP, Schwartz LH. Variability in assessing treatment response: metastatic colorectal cancer as a paradigm. Clin Cancer Res 2014;20(13):3560-3568.
problem: Sources and magnitude of discordance in response assessment of metastatic colorectal cancer.
method: Three radiologists selected RECIST targets and measured unidimensional, bidimensional and volumetric size at baseline and 6 weeks, independently and on the same lesions; linear mixed-effects models of relative change.
data: 29 trial patients; 198 target lesions (about 50-60% liver, 30% lung, 8-12% lymph nodes).
main_result: Variability of relative change: 11% (uni), 19% (bi), 22% (volume) with independent selection; 8%, 14%, 12% on the same lesions. Proposes variability-based cut-offs of +/-30% for volume and states that 'the spherical relationships among the cut-off values ... do not seem to exist'.
relevance: Non-lung (liver-dominant) reader-variability scale for volumetric change to set beside the lung repeat-scan benchmarks; independent support that sphere-converted thresholds are a convention.
not_established: Inter-reader on the same scans, not scan-rescan; small cohort; cut-offs not validated against outcome.

citation: Yoon SH, Kim KW, Goo JM, Kim DW, Hahn S. Observer variability in RECIST-based tumour burden measurements: a meta-analysis. Eur J Cancer 2016;53:5-15.
problem: Size of observer variability in manual RECIST measurements.
method: Systematic search and random-effects meta-analysis of 95% limits of agreement of relative measurement difference.
data: 12 studies of manual CT measurement under RECIST.
main_result: Interobserver limits for single-lesion longest diameter -22.1% to +25.4%; for sums of lesions -19.2% to +19.5%; single-observer sums -9.8% to +13.1%; interobserver interval change of a single lesion -31.3% to +30.3%, which may exceed the 20% progression cut-off.
relevance: Canonical measurement-variability benchmark absent from the response-category comparison ('the major known ones').
not_established: Manual diameters; no category-change rates; abstract only.

citation: Joskowicz L, Cohen D, Caplan N, Sosna J. Inter-observer variability of manual contour delineation of structures in CT. Eur Radiol 2019;29(3):1391-1399.
problem: Inter-observer variability of manual CT delineation as a reference for volumetry and algorithm evaluation.
method: Eleven radiologists delineated 3193 contours; standard volume metrics and group-wise variability metrics.
data: Liver tumours (896 contours), lung tumours (1085), kidneys (434) and brain haematomas (497) on 490 CT slices.
main_result: Between two observers, mean volume difference 7.0% for liver tumours and 10.2% for lung tumours, and mean volume-overlap variability 17.8% and 20.8%; 5%-57% for any two observers; two or three observers capture only part of the total variability; a single observer's delineation "may exhibit these wide variability ranges".
relevance: Quantifies the reference noise behind 'one manual annotation per timepoint' in the limitations, including liver tumours. Cited 13 Oct beside Hering 2024 after 'reference noise' (no extra words).
not_established: Single timepoint, so no change over time; 18 cases from one institution (5 liver- and 5 lung-tumour cases delineated on every slice; kidneys on selected slices); full text checked 13 Oct (version of record, obtained by the user from the authors). Corrected from the abstract-based card, which called it slice-level: the tumour volumes are whole-lesion volumes.

citation: Renard F, Guedria S, De Palma N, Vuillerme N. Variability and reproducibility in deep learning for medical image segmentation. Sci Rep 2020;10:13724.
problem: Sources of variability that threaten the reproducibility of deep-learning medical image segmentation.
method: Literature review of 23 deep-learning segmentation articles against variability and reporting criteria; recommendations.
data: Published articles.
main_result: Variability arises from data, optimisation, hyperparameters, architecture and infrastructure; of the 23 articles only one addressed optimisation variability (by ensembling); recommends several training trials with the same hyperparameters and data, reporting mean and SD.
relevance: Medical-segmentation counterpart of Bouthillier 2021 for the training-run replication rationale; answers the brief's 'Renard 2020, if it exists' (it does).
not_established: No experiments; no update or longitudinal analysis.

citation: Dayma K, Patel P, Hildreth K, Jamaspishvili T. Predetermined change control plan adoption and documentation transparency in U.S. Food and Drug Administration-cleared radiology artificial intelligence/machine learning devices. Radiol Artif Intell 2026;8(5):e260385.
problem: Uptake and transparency of predetermined change control plans (PCCPs) among FDA-cleared radiology AI devices.
method: Cross-sectional scoping review of FDA AI/ML device databases to April 2026; eight-point documentation rubric (ICC 0.93).
data: 1394 AI/ML submissions (1080 radiology); 170 PCCP devices, 37 in radiology.
main_result: 34 of 37 radiology PCCPs were AI/ML-specific, 22 of 34 cleared in 2025; mean documentation score 5 of 8; 'most modifications focused on data retraining, compatibility expansion, and algorithm optimization'; monitoring and drift triggers absent from public summaries.
relevance: Evidence that retraining, the update simulated here, is the most common planned modification of cleared radiology AI; answers a likely 'is the update realistic?' objection.
not_established: Public summaries only; shares of modification types not given in the abstract; abstract only.

citation: Bland JM, Altman DG. Agreement between methods of measurement with multiple observations per individual. J Biopharm Stat 2007;17(4):571-582.
venue_and_status: Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics 17(4):571-582; published; author version on White Rose eprints
problem: Limits of agreement when individuals contribute repeated or clustered pairs of measurements.
method: Variance-component methods for repeated pairs when the true value changes and for replicates when it does not.
data: Worked examples.
main_result: Methods for limits of agreement with clustered observations, for changing and unchanging underlying values (abstract).
relevance: The between-version limits of agreement pool several lesion pairs per patient over 10-20 runs; this is the standard reference for limits with clustered data and pre-empts a statistical objection to citing Bland and Altman 1986 alone.
not_established: Cite only if the computation matches (otherwise describe the method); abstract only; two letters to the editor (Jones 2019; Matsubayashi 2021) report arithmetic and example inconsistencies in the paper.

citation: Tromp J, Bauer D, Claggett BL, Frost M, Iversen MB, Prasad N, Petrie MC, Larson MG, Ezekowitz JA, Solomon SD. A formal validation of a deep learning-based automated workflow for the interpretation of the echocardiogram. Nat Commun 2022;13:6776.
problem: Whether deep-learning echocardiographic measurements can replace core-laboratory human measurements.
method: Individual equivalence coefficient (IEC): disagreement between deep learning and human readers relative to disagreement among three repeated core-lab measurements; prespecified non-inferiority bound of 0.25 for the upper 95% confidence limit.
data: 602 echocardiographic studies from 600 people; 23 parameters including volumes and ejection fraction.
main_result: All IEC point estimates were below 0 and upper limits below 0.25: disagreement between deep learning and humans was lower than among three core-lab readers.
relevance: Deep-learning precedent for a scaled-disagreement index with an a priori acceptance bound; shows how a kappa threshold could be prespecified (the manuscript states 'We set no clinical margin').
not_established: Echocardiography, not CT; no model update or longitudinal change; abstract only.

citation: Omoumi P, Obuchowski NA. How to show that a new imaging method can replace a standard method, when no reference standard is available? Eur Radiol 2022;32(4):2810-2812.
problem: Approaches commonly used to show that a new imaging method can replace a standard one can mislead.
method: Statistical commentary illustrated with four degenerative-spine MRI studies.
data: Four published studies.
main_result: Interchangeability: first quantify how well the current test agrees with itself, then compare with how well the new test agrees with the current one; the definition of agreement and the maximum allowable difference must be set a priori; applies to qualitative and quantitative data (cites Obuchowski 2014 and Barnhart 2007).
relevance: Open-access, radiology-facing summary of the logic behind kappa and recommendation (2); supports prespecifying an allowable excess disagreement.
not_established: Short commentary; no AI updates or change measurement.

citation: Therasse P, Arbuck SG, Eisenhauer EA, Wanders J, Kaplan RS, Rubinstein L, et al. New guidelines to evaluate the response to treatment in solid tumors. J Natl Cancer Inst 2000;92(3):205-216.
venue_and_status: Journal of the National Cancer Institute 92(3):205-216; published (OUP)
problem: Replace the WHO bidimensional criteria with unidimensional response criteria (RECIST 1.0).
method: Consensus guideline of the EORTC, NCI (USA) and NCI Canada.
data: n/a
main_result: Introduced RECIST. According to Wesdorp et al. 2021 (full text read, R-S013), it defines the geometric relation of a 30% diameter decrease to a 65% volume decrease and a 20% increase to a 73% volume increase.
relevance: Original source of the sphere-volume equivalents (-65%/+73%) that the manuscript computes as -65.7%/+72.8% and currently attributes to RECIST 1.1 (eisenhauer2009).
not_established: Full text blocked (Cloudflare 403); the volume relation was verified only through a secondary source; RECIST 1.1 itself states the 73% equivalence (per Costelloe 2010).

citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Technical performance assessment of quantitative imaging in radiological device premarket submissions: guidance for industry and Food and Drug Administration staff. Silver Spring, MD: FDA; 16 June 2022 (docket FDA-2019-D-1470). https://www.fda.gov/media/123271/download
venue_and_status: FDA final guidance (nonbinding), issued 16 June 2022; draft 19 April 2019
problem: Technical-performance information that premarket submissions with quantitative imaging functions should contain.
method: Regulatory guidance.
data: n/a
main_result: Lists typical sources of error in quantitative imaging values, including image-processing 'Algorithm specifics (e.g., filtering, software version, database selection)' and 'Non-deterministic algorithm'; asks for the name and version of the software platform; defines repeatability and reproducibility.
relevance: Regulatory statement that software version is a source of measurement error; a zero-word addition to 'That software changes can alter quantitative imaging measurements is well documented'.
not_established: Premarket, single-version focus; says nothing about mixing versions across follow-up.

citation: Paal M, Habler K, Vogeser M. Estimation of inter-laboratory reference change values from external quality assessment data. Biochem Med (Zagreb) 2021;31(3):030902.
problem: Interpreting serial laboratory results obtained in different laboratories when patients switch providers.
method: Inter-laboratory reference change values from external quality assessment CVs and within-subject biological variation, using log-transformed asymmetric limits.
data: 2019 external quality assessment data for creatinine, calcium, aldosterone, PSA and HbA1c; EFLM biological-variation data.
main_result: Inter-laboratory reference change values ranged from +13.3% to +203% and -11.8% to -67.0%, differing substantially between analytes.
relevance: Laboratory-medicine analogue of change measured across measuring systems: the critical difference for serial results widens when the measuring system differs; pre-empts a 'this is known from laboratory medicine' objection and points to the reference change value literature (Fraser 2011, R-S033).
not_established: Laboratory analytes with additive variance assumptions; no imaging; abstract only.
code_or_data: uses public EQA and EFLM data

citation: D'Amour A, Heller K, Moldovan D, Adlam B, Alipanahi B, Beutel A, et al. Underspecification presents challenges for credibility in modern machine learning. J Mach Learn Res 2022;23(226):1-61.
venue_and_status: Journal of Machine Learning Research 23(226):1-61; published (no DOI)
problem: Why models with equivalent held-out performance behave differently in deployment.
method: Defines underspecification; stress tests of pipelines that differ only in arbitrary choices such as the random seed.
data: Examples from computer vision, medical imaging, natural language processing, clinical risk prediction and genomics.
main_result: Underspecified pipelines return many predictors with equivalently strong held-out performance that behave very differently in deployment domains.
relevance: General account of why training runs with similar Dice differ in volume shift, and why 'each deployed checkpoint needs its own check'.
not_established: No segmentation volumetry or updates; abstract only.
